vocab.title: Match each term to its meaning

a plan prepared in advance for something that may go wrong
a practice exercise that rehearses an emergency procedure
a source of danger that exists before anything has gone wrong
an official list of steps that has to be verified item by item
an action taken in advance to stop an incident from happening
the formal act of telling an authority that something has happened
the official step-by-step sequence for doing something on board
a failure of equipment to work as it should
a formal notification that something needs attention now

reading.rtitle: The Alarm Nobody Stopped to Read
paras: The general alarm on the main switchboard sounded at 0341 and continued for eleven minutes. The officer of the watch stopped monitoring it after the second minute, having decided that the malfunction was in the sensor rather than in the circuit. He did not stop to read the fault code, which would have taken about fifteen seconds and would have told him the opposite.

The company's own procedure is explicit. On any repeated alarm the watchkeeper is to record the code, notify the engine room and, if the alert persists beyond five minutes, wake the chief engineer. The pre-departure checklist covering that switchboard had been signed three days earlier. Investigators found no evidence that it had been worked through, and the officer, when asked, said he remembered signing it but did not remember checking anything.

The deviation that followed was small and expensive. With the alarm still sounding, the master elected to try running the affected section on the emergency generator, a step the contingency plan does not contain. It worked for forty minutes and then did not, and the vessel lost steering for a little over two minutes in a channel where two minutes is the whole margin.

The report is careful with its language. It notes that the officer regretted not reading the code, and that he had been on watch for eleven hours. It records that notification to the company was delayed by four hours and that the delay has not been explained. It concludes that the hazard was known, the procedure existed, the checklist had been signed, and none of those three facts had any effect whatever on what happened at 0341.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- engineering casualty report written for this lesson in the register of the PS-ASON reading passages

gist.prompt: What is the point the report is making?
choices: That the emergency generator was the wrong equipment for the job.
That the procedure, the checklist and the knowledge all existed and none of them changed what was done.
That the officer should have been relieved after eight hours on watch.

items: The officer paused in order to read the fault code.
The text says he 'did not stop to read the fault code'. Stop to do means pause in order to do it -- and he did not.
The officer ceased watching the alarm two minutes after it began.
The text says he 'stopped monitoring it after the second minute'. Stop doing means cease the activity.
The officer recalled having signed the checklist.
The text says he 'remembered signing it but did not remember checking anything'.
Running the section on the emergency generator was a step foreseen in the contingency plan.
The text says it was 'a step the contingency plan does not contain'.
The company was informed without delay.
The text says 'notification to the company was delayed by four hours and the delay has not been explained'.

items.situation: He stopped monitoring the alarm. Is he watching it now?
tips: No. Stop doing means the activity ended.
Stop to do would mean he paused in order to watch it.

items.situation: He remembered signing the checklist. Did he sign it before or after remembering?
tips: Before. Remember doing looks back at a completed action.
Remember to do looks forward at an obligation.

items.situation: Say the difference between he tried to restart it and he tried restarting it.
tips: Tried to restart: he attempted something difficult, maybe without success.
Tried restarting: he used restarting as a method to see whether it would help.

items.situation: An option says: the officer stopped to read the fault code. Is that in the text?
tips: No, the opposite. The text says he did NOT stop to read it.
One word of difference and the fact reverses.

items.situation: Say, in exam register, that nobody told the company for four hours.
tips: Notification to the company was delayed by four hours.
The company was not informed until four hours later.

items.situation: We regret to inform you. Is the writer sorry about something already done, or announcing bad news?
tips: Announcing bad news. Regret to inform is a fixed formal opening.
Regret informing would mean he was sorry he had told you.

listenings.text: I want to be accurate about this, because I have heard it repeated wrongly. I did not ignore the alarm. I watched it for two minutes, I decided it was the sensor, and then I stopped watching it. Those are two different things and only one of them is what I did. What I did not do, and what I regret, is stop to read the fault code. Fifteen seconds. The code would have told me the fault was in the circuit and I would have called the engine room at three forty-three instead of at four fifty. And yes, I had been on watch for eleven hours, and no, I am not offering that as an explanation. Plenty of people do eleven hours and read the code. I remember signing the checklist. I do not remember checking a single item on it, and I have said so from the first interview.

Every checklist starts as a procedure and ends as a signature, and the interval is usually about two years. The first time a form is used, somebody walks the deck with it. The fiftieth time, somebody signs it in the office because he already knows what it says. And he does know. That is the uncomfortable part: the people who sign without checking are usually the ones who understand the system best. So we stopped adding items. Adding items is what everybody tries first, and it makes the problem worse, because the longer the form the faster it is signed. What we do now is change one item every month, without announcing which. If you have actually worked through the list, you notice. If you have remembered to sign it, you do not.
